facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Leverage has fallen because earnings recovered while debt stayed flat. Derived EBITDA rose from 152.276 US$m in FY2024 to 353.246 US$m in FY2025 and 536.582 US$m for the last twelve months, while carrying debt moved only from 990.587 to 993.606 US$m, so gross leverage went from 6.51x to 2.81x to 1.85x. The mechanism is operating leverage on a largely fixed cost base after the 2023 restructuring, and it matters to creditors because the improvement came from profit, not from repaying the notes; a profit setback would raise leverage again without any change in debt. Basis: calculation C28; calculation C31; calculation C34; calculation C13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3

facts.label: Company description and credit linkage
facts.text: Twilio sells communications and customer-data software to businesses: programmable messaging, voice and email interfaces that let customers send and receive messages and calls, plus customer data, authentication and engagement products. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is repeat usage rather than contracted revenue: usage fees were 74% of FY2025 revenue and 76% of third-quarter 2026 revenue, the ten largest accounts were 9%, and existing customers expanded spending at 108% in FY2025 and 114% in the latest quarter. The risk mechanic is volume: customers' own usage drives revenue, so macro weakness or product substitution lowers revenue faster than a subscription business would, and the issuer itself says usage-based revenue is more immediately affected. Contracted visibility is thin, with remaining performance obligations equal to 2.07% of annual revenue. Pricing power is mixed: gross margin held at 49% in FY2025 against 51% in FY2024 while growth was 14%, but some competitors have lower list prices and carrier fee increases were passed through at cost, so revenue growth excluding those fees was 12.55% in FY2025 and 15.84% in the latest quarter. Revenue is therefore cyclical and discretionary at the margin, concentrated in Messaging at 56.80%, and not structurally declining. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Cost of revenue is mostly fees paid to network service providers, so gross margin follows carrier and cloud pricing, and pass-through of higher carrier fees raises revenue and cost equally, which dilutes margin without changing gross profit. Operating expenses consist primarily of personnel costs: they were 45.80% of revenue in FY2025 against 52.31% in FY2024, so derived EBITDA rose with gross profit and the incremental operating margin in nine months 2026 was 31.38%. Margins can be defended against volume pressure only partly: a fall of 18.94% in gross profit would remove all derived EBITDA with costs unchanged, but management has cut costs before, reducing sales and marketing expense by 15.85% from FY2023 to FY2024, which is the lever that would be used first. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 83, 87–89; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation C14; calculation C16; calculation C18; calculation C17

facts.label: Capital intensity and FCF conversion
facts.text: Capital intensity is low: capitalized software and long-lived asset purchases were 1.14% of FY2025 revenue, and cash taxes were only USD 25.74 million in nine months 2026, so almost all operating cash flow is free cash flow, USD 945 million in FY2025 and USD 1.11 billion for the last twelve months. facts.label: Porter's Five Forces
facts.text: Rivalry is real and rising: the issuer names CPaaS companies, regional carriers with developer tools, customer-experience and customer-data vendors as rivals, expects competition to intensify, and says some rivals have lower list prices, which if matched would lower gross profit against a fixed cost base. Entry pressure comes at the edges, since new market entrants and software vendors target parts of the product line, but breadth across messaging, voice, email and data is not matched by any one rival, which protects the core. Substitutes are the sharpest threat to authentication and messaging volumes, for example if one-time passwords are phased out or over-the-top channels such as WhatsApp and RCS shift traffic, although Twilio sells those channels itself. Buyer power is limited by diversification, with the ten largest accounts at 9% of revenue, but developers can switch and may reduce or delay spending. Supplier power is high: carriers and one cloud provider are hard to replace, many carriers have no long-term contracts, and fee rises are passed on only to the extent customers accept them. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12, 26, 29–30, 34, 47, 87

facts.label: PEST analysis
facts.text: Four factors alter credit capacity. Regulatory exposure is real but contained: Twilio ended service to Iran-linked entities in March 2025 without receiving revenue from them, and telecommunications, privacy and sanctions rules govern its channels. Economic exposure is the usage model, which the issuer says is more immediately hit by weak macro conditions, tariffs and inflation than subscription revenue. Technological change cuts both ways, since AI products and new channels such as RCS add volume while changes to authentication practice could reduce it. Political factors act through trade policy and sanctions risk, with no figure that moves the credit view. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 19, 26–27, 149; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15

facts.label: Financial profile and credit quality
facts.text: Scale and market position are strong in the sense that matters to creditors: USD 5.07 billion of revenue, many customers and a platform the issuer says no single rival matches in breadth. Competitive advantage is average, because it rests on breadth, deliverability and integration rather than contracts, and the filings supply no market share or switching evidence beyond expansion of 108%. Diversification is average: customers and geography are spread, with the ten largest at 9% and International at 36%, but Messaging is 56.80% of revenue. Cost and capex flexibility is strong, with 1.14% capital intensity and a record of cost cuts. Margin stability is weak: gross margin moved from 49% to 51% and back to 49%, and derived EBITDA margin is 9.20%. Free cash flow stability is average, because the cash is reliable but USD 41 million of it remained after stock-based compensation in FY2024. Refinancing and market access is strong given the 2.89x cash cover and the 2029 maturity. Liquidity is strong, with USD 2.89 billion of cash and securities and no facility to refinance or draw. Financial policy and governance is average: no debt-funded distribution and a clean audit, but large repurchases and unknown indenture limits and board detail. The trend is improving on leverage and margin, with the main missing items being the indenture, the commitment schedule and competitor data. facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over the next 12 to 24 months the evidence favours continued cash generation: revenue grew 20% in the latest quarter, or 15.84% excluding carrier fees, expansion was 114%, and operating expenses rose only 3.51% in the quarter against revenue growth of 20%. Headwinds are that pass-through revenue dilutes margin, purchase commitments of USD 1.3 billion call on cash, repurchases continue, and the Syniverse stake still produces losses. Over three to five years the 2029 and 2031 notes fall due, and the cash cushion means they can be repaid or refinanced on the issuer's terms; the tailwind is rising usage by existing customers, as the expansion rate shows, and new channels such as RCS, and the headwind is price competition and possible substitution of one-time passwords. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The initiating condition is a further round of carrier fee increases that customers resist, combined with price competition in messaging. The first operational break is gross margin: cost of revenue, mostly network fees, rises faster than revenue, so gross profit falls. The financial transmission is fast because operating expenses are largely fixed; with operating costs unchanged, a 10% fall in last-twelve-month gross profit takes derived EBITDA from USD 537 million to USD 253 million, lifts total debt to derived EBITDA to 3.92x and cuts cover to 6.75x, and a fall of 18.94% would remove all derived EBITDA. Free cash flow would fall by the same amount before tax effects, to about USD 827 million, which still covers cash interest many times over. The liquidity and refinancing consequence is limited: cash and securities of USD 2.89 billion cover the notes 2.89x before any free cash flow, nothing falls due until 2029, and management could stop repurchases, which have USD 698.7 million of authorisation left, or cut sales and marketing cost as in 2024. Resilience therefore appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress; the observable triggers are gross profit falling while revenue grows, cash and securities falling towards USD 2.0 billion, and repurchases above free cash flow. This is an illustration labelled as analyst judgement, not a forecast. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34, 83, 87, 89; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 13, 39; calculation C18; calculation C19; calculation C20; calculation C21; calculation C22; calculation C36

## Findings
### Bottom line

The supplied filings are enough for a full financial, liquidity and business analysis of Twilio Inc, but not for legal, covenant, ratings or pricing work, so creditor protections can be read only from the issuer's own summary of the notes. The borrowings are two series of unsecured senior notes due 2029 and 2031 with only minor finance leases besides, and no credit facility, letter of credit or other bank commitment is disclosed, so the main liquidity inputs are printed. The indentures, the proxy statement, earnings releases, ratings and trading levels were not supplied, and nothing dated after the Q3 filing of 2026-10-30 was supplied.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Twilio's two senior note series are small against recovered earnings and fully covered by cash, with gross leverage on derived reported EBITDA falling from 6.51x for FY2024 to 1.85x for the last twelve months to Q3 2026, so debt service is not a near-term constraint.
Basis: calculation C28; calculation C34; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 13

That improvement rests on an EBITDA derived from operating income and depreciation, because the issuer reports none, and on profits that followed large impairments and restructuring charges in 2023. Net income for the first nine months of 2026 is inflated by a non-cash tax benefit and is not a guide to cash earnings, and the issuer's summary of the notes lists no limit on share repurchases, though the indenture was not supplied, so cash can be returned to shareholders unless the full terms say otherwise.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 135–136; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 27; calculation C06; calculation C07

### Financial interpretation

Leverage has fallen because earnings recovered while debt stayed flat. Derived EBITDA rose from 152.276 US$m in FY2024 to 353.246 US$m in FY2025 and 536.582 US$m for the last twelve months, while carrying debt moved only from 990.587 to 993.606 US$m, so gross leverage went from 6.51x to 2.81x to 1.85x. The mechanism is operating leverage on a largely fixed cost base after the 2023 restructuring, and it matters to creditors because the improvement came from profit, not from repaying the notes; a profit setback would raise leverage again without any change in debt.
Basis: calculation C28; calculation C31; calculation C34; calculation C13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3

Coverage is ample and set by the fixed coupons. Cash interest paid has stayed near 37.578 US$m a year, which matches the scheduled coupons of 37.5 US$m (calculation C45), and EBITDA cover rose from 4.02x in FY2024 to 9.40x and 14.30x on the last twelve months. Because the notes are fixed rate and the investments are short dated, interest cost does not rise if rates rise; the FY2023 cover is negative only because impairments and restructuring charges drove operating income below zero.
Basis: calculation C30; calculation C33; calculation C36; calculation C45; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 43

Cash conversion is strong but flattered by non-cash compensation. Operating cash flow of 1003.244 US$m in FY2025 exceeded derived EBITDA by 649.998 US$m because stock-based compensation of 600.407 US$m is an expense that does not use cash, and free cash flow on the issuer's definition was 945.427 US$m. That cash has gone mainly to share repurchases of 868.939 US$m in FY2025 and 448.296 US$m in nine months 2026, so cash and securities have rebuilt since the end of 2024 while capital allocation, not debt repayment, remains the main use; for creditors the point is that nothing in the stated covenants stops further buybacks.

Basis: calculation C47; calculation C18; 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 106–108; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6; 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 135–136

Liquidity is the main strength, with limits around commitments. Cash and cash equivalents were 1061.531 US$m and short-term marketable securities 1829.94 US$m at 2026-09-30, against notes that fall due in 2029 and 2031 and no credit facility to draw or to refinance. The weak point is outside the debt: purchase commitments are reported as a single USD 1.3 billion total at 2026-09-30, up from USD 349.241 million at the end of 2025, with no yearly schedule, so the pace at which that cash is called is not established. Operating lease liabilities of 63.394 US$m are outside Total Debt.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 15; 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 137; calculation C41; calculation C43

The only named non-debt funding float is deferred revenue and customer deposits of 157.046 US$m at 2026-09-30, against 158.677 at 2025-12-31 and 155.68 at 2024-12-31, which is small and flat, so a customer-driven drawdown of that float is not a near-term funding risk. Accrued cost of revenue of 285.224 US$m, up from 226.878 US$m at the year end, behaves like a supplier payable for network and infrastructure costs.

In the latest quarter the only financing-type events are share repurchases: USD 127.2 million of stock was bought in the third quarter of 2026 and USD 446.7 million in nine months, leaving USD 698.7 million of the USD 2.0 billion authorisation, which expires at the end of 2027. No debt was issued or repaid, no amendment to the notes is described, no consent decree or settlement is described, and the latest acquisition was the USD 104.1 million cash purchase of Stytch in November 2025; the 43.7% Syniverse stake is an equity-method investment whose own debt is outside Twilio's.

Claims outside debt are small except for purchase commitments. Operating lease liabilities of 63.394 US$m sit outside Total Debt, accrued non-income taxes were 24.0 US$m domestic and 22.0 US$m foreign at 2026-09-30, and unrecognized tax benefits were 280.7 US$m at 2025-12-31, of which only 1.3 US$m would affect the effective tax rate. No pension, retiree medical, factoring, supplier-finance or consent-decree funding obligation is described, and the summary of the notes lists no financial maintenance test, so there is no reported covenant headroom to state.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 135–136, 146; calculation C43

Data quality is good for the statements and weaker for the earnings measure. The balance sheet, cash flow and income statement identities reconcile exactly for every period in the tables, but EBITDA and interest expense are not reported by the issuer, so leverage and cover rest on a derived EBITDA with no add-backs, and the fourth quarter of 2025 exists only by subtraction. The nine-month 2026 net income of 1318.505 US$m includes a tax benefit of 937.077 US$m from releasing the valuation allowance, a non-cash event, so earnings per share and return ratios for 2026 should not be read as cash earnings.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 5–6, 27; calculation C46; calculation C22

The most material gaps are the commitment schedule and the legal terms. Without the indenture, the lien and merger covenants are known only from the issuer's summary, and without a commitment schedule the cash calls on the large 2026 commitments cannot be dated; the leverage picture is otherwise well supported.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 135–136, 137; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; Source readiness (CP-0)

## Gaps

- Interest expense and interest income are not printed separately in any of the five filings because both sit within other income, net, for every period; this restricts interest coverage to cash interest paid and prevents a split of net interest, severity Low, and the action that would close it is a note or earnings release that splits other income.

- EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA are not reported by the issuer for any period, so the reported EBITDA row is derived from operating income plus depreciation and amortization and the adjusted EBITDA row and bridge are not stated, severity Medium, and the action is an issuer earnings release or management bridge.

- Reported EBITDA is negative for FY2023 after large impairment and restructuring charges, so leverage for FY2023 is not calculable and the cover figure is negative, severity Low, and no action is needed beyond reading the 2023 figure as an outlier.

- The fourth quarter of 2025 is not reported separately, so revenue, operating income and EBITDA for that quarter exist only as the FY2025 figure less the nine-month 2025 comparative, severity Low, and the action is the issuer's fourth-quarter release.

- The nine-month non-GAAP reconciliation is not printed in the third-quarter report, which gives three months only, so nine-month add-backs are not stated beyond the cash flow lines, severity Low, and the action is to assemble them from the three quarterly reports.

- Several line items are not printed in some periods: restructuring and long-lived asset impairment lines do not appear in the nine-month income statements, the prepaid asset impairment appears only in 2026, and some investing, financing and non-cash lines appear in the annual statements only; these cells are marked as not supplied and nothing is set to zero, severity Low, and no action is needed.

- Source dashes were left as missing, not zero, for lines such as the foreign exchange effect on cash in FY2024 and FY2025, the FY2024 long-lived asset impairment, the equity-method impairment in FY2023 and FY2024 and acquisitions or divestitures in some years, severity Low, and the action is none because the filings print no amount.

- The deferred tax asset is not a separate balance-sheet line in the annual report or the first-quarter report; the later reports show 20026 thousand at 2025-12-31 inside the 242674 thousand shown in the annual report, so the FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 deferred tax asset cells are not supplied, severity Low, and the action is none beyond the stated reclassification.

- Net debt on cash and equivalents alone understates liquidity because short-term marketable securities are a large part of the liquid assets, so the wider figure is stated beside it, severity Low, and no action is needed.

- Purchase commitments are single totals in each quarterly report with no yearly schedule and a large unexplained step up between the first and second quarters of 2026, so claims outside debt for 2026 cannot be scheduled, severity Medium, and the action is the commitment schedule and counterparty from the issuer.

- No committed credit facility, letter of credit or other undrawn facility is disclosed in any filing, so undrawn committed facilities are not supplied in the liquidity table; this is a finding from a search of all five filings, not a missing document, severity Low, and no action is needed.

- The indenture and first supplemental indenture are not supplied, so covenant definitions, baskets and guarantee triggers are known only from the annual report summary, which restricts any covenant or priority conclusion, severity Medium, and the action is to supply the executed documents.

- Segment revenue exists only for FY2023 and FY2024 under the earlier two-segment presentation and the issuer reports one segment from the third quarter of 2025, so segment trends cannot be extended, severity Low, and the action is none.

- FY2024 and FY2023 product revenue groups differ between the FY2024 and FY2025 annual reports because of a reclassification, so only the FY2025 report's presentation is used for those years, severity Low, and the action is none.

- Active Customer Accounts was discontinued from the first quarter of 2026, so the customer-count series ends at 402000 at 2025-12-31, severity Low, and the action is to ask the issuer for the figure if it is needed.

- Nothing dated after the third-quarter report of 2026-10-30 is supplied up to the cutoff of 2026-11-18, so events in that window are not established, severity Low, and the action is any current report filed after that date.

- Cash paid for interest in the nine-month 2026 statement is the only interest figure for that period, so last-twelve-months cash interest is built from three cash flow statements and is calculated, severity Low, and no action is needed.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Twilio is a listed issuer with one class of shares and no sponsor named, so creditor risk comes from how management allocates cash, and the filings show large cash-funded buybacks, no debt-funded distribution and no liability-management history.

The operating model is usage-driven with no customer above 10% of revenue, but it depends on carriers and one cloud provider, and the board, ownership and indenture detail that would test creditor protection was not supplied.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34, 47, 110, 149; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Key findings

- **Capital allocation, not control, carries the governance risk.** The company spent USD 2.3 billion on buybacks in 2024, USD 854.6 million in 2025 and USD 446.7 million in the first nine months of 2026, always from cash and securities rather than debt, which cut cash and securities from USD 4.0 billion to USD 2.4 billion in 2024 while the two note series stayed unchanged. The effect on creditors is a thinner cushion, not higher leverage, and nothing in the issuer's summary of the notes limits repurchases.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 135–136, 140; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 39; calculation C13

- **The notes have been static since 2021, which keeps refinancing risk distant but untested.** The two series total USD 1.0 billion, nothing was issued, exchanged, amended or repaid in the periods read, and the first maturity is in 2029; with no credit facility and no rating stated, there is no market or lender test of the issuer's behaviour under stress.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 135–136; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 13; calculation C18

- **Demand risk is spread but volume-sensitive.** No customer exceeded 10% of revenue in 2023 to 2025, yet usage-based fees were 74% of FY2025 revenue and 76% of third-quarter 2026 revenue, so spending cuts by many customers would show in revenue quickly, with fourth-quarter seasonality adding to quarterly swings.

- **Supplier dependence is the sharper operating risk.** The company outsources the substantial majority of its cloud infrastructure to one provider, many carriers and network providers have no long-term contracts, and carrier messaging fee increases are passed on at cost, which lowers gross margin without changing gross profit; an outage or terms change at a supplier would hit service and cost directly.

- **Messaging dominates the revenue base.** Messaging was 56.80% of FY2025 revenue and grew 18.18% on the regrouped prior year, the fastest of the product groups, so credit quality tracks one usage product that is also the most exposed to carrier fees; international revenue was 36%.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 136; calculation C01; calculation C07; calculation C06

- **Acquisitions are small and cash-funded, and the large equity stake has been a drag.** Stytch cost USD 104.1 million in cash in November 2025, while the 2022 purchase of a minority stake in Syniverse for USD 750.0 million was impaired by USD 80.6 million in FY2025 and still reduces earnings through equity-method losses; the filings describe no Twilio guarantee of the investee's debt.

- **Board, ownership and pay detail is the main gap.** The annual report defers Part III to a proxy statement that was not supplied, so only the signing directors and officers are known and no holder concentration, committee structure or control right can be assessed.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 149, 152; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a benign view is the scale of the 2024 buyback: cash repurchases were 3.55x free cash flow that year and were met by running down short-term securities, so the same behaviour could be repeated, and the issuer's summary of the notes lists no covenant that would stop it. The reassurance is that cash and securities still cover the notes 2.89x and the buyback pace has since fallen to 0.92x of free cash flow in 2025 and 0.52x in the first nine months of 2026.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 93, 107, 140; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 6, 13; calculation C14; calculation C15; calculation C16; calculation C17

The view would worsen if the company funded a buyback or acquisition with new debt, issued secured debt or a credit facility ahead of the notes, or amended the indenture, and it would improve if the executed indenture showed limits on distributions, liens and subsidiary guarantees or if the proxy statement showed independent oversight of capital allocation.
### Limitations

- The proxy statement was not supplied, so board independence, committee structure, pay design, voting rights and holder concentration are not established, which keeps the governance risk level at Medium and blocks any conclusion on ownership concentration.

- The indenture was not supplied, so whether the notes restrict repurchases, asset sales or subsidiary guarantees beyond the issuer's summary is not established, which leaves the link between legal capacity and behaviour open and keeps any covenant-based conclusion out of this module.

- No earnings release, guidance or management commentary was supplied, so management's own account of capital allocation priorities rests on the strategy section of the annual report and cannot be tested against guidance.

- Dated market data and ratings were not supplied, so market reaction to buybacks and the notes' pricing are not established, which limits how far the cash-funded repurchase record can be read as creditor-aligned.
### Governance view

Overall, Twilio presents medium governance risk for creditors. The key supported behaviour is the repeated cash-funded repurchase of shares, which matters because it reduces the cash and securities that back the notes while leaving debt unchanged, and it implies a thinner liquidity cushion rather than higher leverage. Countervailing evidence is the absence of any debt-funded distribution, dividend, amendment or exchange, the clean audit opinion on the statements and internal control, and cash and securities that still exceed the notes. Further analysis requires the proxy statement, the executed indenture and any guidance document. Governance assessment completed with limitations; risk level Medium; key gaps are board and ownership detail, indenture terms and management guidance.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Twilio's fundamental credit profile is adequate to strong, because net cash, a distant first maturity and strong cash generation outweigh thin margins and low contract visibility, so note holders face little near-term default risk and the main danger is shareholder-friendly policy rather than operating stress.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 13; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C33; calculation C36

The business is a large, usage-priced messaging platform whose derived earnings are small against its cost base, and the notes' summarised terms list no limit on the heavy share repurchases of the past three years. A squeeze from carrier or cloud costs or a slowdown in customer volumes would be met first by the cash cushion, which is why liquidity and shareholder payouts are the right things to monitor.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34, 87, 135–136; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C13; calculation C41
### Key findings

- **Liquidity and leverage are the anchor of the credit.** Cash and short-term securities of USD 2.89 billion cover the USD 1.0 billion of senior notes 2.89x, and gross debt to derived EBITDA fell from 6.51x in FY2024 to 2.81x in FY2025 and 1.85x for the last twelve months, with cover of 14.30x on fixed coupons. The first maturity is about 28 months away and the 2029 notes can already be redeemed at par, so refinancing is a choice rather than a risk.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 135–136; calculation C35; calculation C36; calculation C33; calculation C31; calculation C32; calculation C34; calculation C46

- **Cash generation is strong but flattered by non-cash pay.** Free cash flow of USD 945 million in FY2025 and USD 1.11 billion for the last twelve months is 2.68x and 2.07x derived EBITDA because stock-based compensation of USD 600 million is deducted in earnings but not paid in cash; after that charge free cash flow was USD 345 million in FY2025 and only USD 41 million in FY2024. For creditors this means true cash earnings are real but smaller than the headline, and buybacks that merely offset dilution are a recurring use of that cash.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 89, 93, 107; calculation C27; calculation C28; calculation C23; calculation C24; calculation C25; calculation C26

- **Margins are thin and operating leverage cuts both ways.** Derived EBITDA margin rose from 3.42% in FY2024 to 6.97% in FY2025 and 9.20% for the last twelve months because operating expenses were flat in FY2025 and grew far more slowly than revenue in nine months 2026, giving an incremental operating margin of 31.38% in nine months 2026; the same fixed cost base means a fall of 18.94% in gross profit would remove all derived EBITDA.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 89; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation C12; calculation C11; calculation C13; calculation C14; calculation C16; calculation C18

- **Revenue is broad but short on contractual visibility.** No customer exceeds 10% of revenue and the ten largest are 9%, and expansion by existing customers was 108% in FY2025 and 114% in the latest quarter, yet usage-based fees are 74% of revenue and remaining performance obligations are only 2.07% of last-twelve-month revenue, so a volume or pricing shock would show in revenue within a quarter.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 84, 87, 110; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 32; calculation C08; calculation C01

- **Messaging and its suppliers are the concentration that matters.** Messaging is 56.80% of revenue, the carriers behind it raised fees from June 2025 and Twilio passes these through at cost, which added USD 49.5 million of revenue in FY2025 and USD 53.1 million in the latest quarter without adding gross profit, so growth excluding these fees was 15.84% against 20% reported. One cloud provider hosts the substantial majority of the platform and many network providers have no long-term contracts.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34, 47, 83, 90, 136; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 32–33; calculation C05; calculation C04

- **Shareholder returns are the main policy risk.** Cash repurchases were 3.55x free cash flow in FY2024, a year in which cash and securities fell by USD 1.63 billion, then fell to 0.92x in FY2025 and 0.52x in nine months 2026, with USD 698.7 million of authorisation left to the end of 2027; the issuer's summary of the notes lists limits on liens, subsidiary guarantees and mergers but none on repurchases.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 93, 107, 135–136, 140; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6, 39; calculation C41; calculation C42; calculation C43; calculation C40

- **Commitments and the Syniverse stake are the leakage to watch.** Purchase commitments are reported as USD 1.3 billion at 2026-09-30, up from USD 349.24 million at 2025-12-31, still 2.22x covered by cash and securities, and the minority stake in Syniverse produced equity-method losses equal to 22.61% of operating income in nine months 2026 after a USD 80.6 million impairment in FY2025, though both are non-core and the stake is carried at USD 225.18 million.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 132, 137; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 3, 15; calculation C39; calculation C47
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against an adequate-to-strong view is how little of Twilio's earnings is protected: derived EBITDA is 9.20% of revenue, remaining performance obligations on multi-year contracts are 2.07% of last-twelve-month revenue, the cost of revenue is mostly fees set by carriers, and free cash flow after stock-based compensation was only USD 41 million in FY2024, so a second round of carrier fee increases that customers refuse to absorb would hit earnings quickly. The cash cushion answers this, but it is also what shareholders have drawn on before: it fell by USD 1.63 billion in 2024.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34, 87, 135–136; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 8; calculation C13; calculation C08; calculation C25; calculation C40

The view would weaken if cash and short-term securities fell below USD 2.0 billion, if repurchases exceeded free cash flow again, if debt were issued to fund them, or if gross profit fell year on year while revenue grew. It would strengthen if the executed indenture showed limits on distributions, if the commitment schedule showed the USD 1.3 billion falling due in line with revenue, and if derived EBITDA margin kept rising above 9.20% without more pass-through revenue.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 13, 15; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C35; calculation C41; calculation C13
### Limitations

- Competitive position rests on the issuer's own description of its rivals because no market share, pricing or peer data was supplied, so the judgement that the platform keeps its pricing and margin position could be too generous if competitors price below it.

- Contract visibility is read from one figure for remaining performance obligations that covers only contracts longer than one year, so the conclusion that revenue visibility is low could overstate the risk if shorter usage commitments recur reliably.

- The monitoring thresholds are anchored on Twilio's own reported history rather than on any covenant, rating criterion or lender test, so crossing one is a prompt to reassess and not a default signal.
- The downside sensitivity holds operating expenses at their latest level, so it overstates the net fall in earnings that would remain after cost cuts like those of 2024, and it uses no forecast.
### Credit view

Overall, Twilio presents an adequate-to-strong business profile supported by net cash, a distant first maturity, low capital intensity and strong free cash flow, but credit quality is constrained by thin derived margins, usage-based revenue with little contractual visibility, dependence on carriers and one cloud provider, and shareholder returns that the notes' summarised terms do not limit. Cash-flow durability appears adequate due to the cash conversion of stock-based pay and the cost levers management has used before. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the cash cushion rather than on market access. The primary downside path is carrier fees or price pressure compressing gross profit against a fixed cost base. Further analysis would require the executed indenture and the commitment schedule. Fundamental credit analysis completed. Top risk: gross profit compression from carrier fees on a fixed cost base.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 13, 15; 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34, 83, 135–136; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C18; calculation C36; calculation C13

### Company description and credit linkage

Twilio sells communications and customer-data software to businesses: programmable messaging, voice and email interfaces that let customers send and receive messages and calls, plus customer data, authentication and engagement products. FY2025 revenue was USD 5.07 billion, growing 14%, from hundreds of thousands of customer accounts; International was 36% of revenue. The credit link is direct: usage fees tie revenue to customers' own message and call volumes, which gives fast growth when volumes rise and little protection when they fall, while the low capital needs mean that earnings convert into cash. The business moved to one reportable segment in 2025, so there is no segment profit to read.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 6–10, 36, 82, 104–105, 136; Business & governance (CP-1A)

Operating history matters to creditors because the business was restructured in 2023, with impairments and restructuring costs that pushed derived EBITDA negative that year, and was then run for profit. Divestitures in 2023, a wind-down in 2024 and one small cash acquisition in November 2025 changed the perimeter little, so the recovered earnings are not the product of acquisitions.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 89, 131; 10-K_2024-12-31_twlo-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 41; Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Ownership and group structure

Twilio is a Delaware company with one class of shares listed in New York, no sponsor or controlling holder named, and nine directors, including the chief executive, who signed the annual report. Share ownership and board independence are not established because the proxy statement was not supplied. The financial-policy consequence is visible in behaviour rather than structure: the share count fell 16.23% between 2023-12-31 and 2025-12-31, no dividend has ever been paid, and there is no parent or sponsor to support the credit. The only investment outside the consolidated group that the filings describe is the minority Syniverse stake, which is equity-accounted, so its debt sits outside Twilio's accounts.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 80, 116, 131–132, 152; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C45
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is repeat usage rather than contracted revenue: usage fees were 74% of FY2025 revenue and 76% of third-quarter 2026 revenue, the ten largest accounts were 9%, and existing customers expanded spending at 108% in FY2025 and 114% in the latest quarter. The risk mechanic is volume: customers' own usage drives revenue, so macro weakness or product substitution lowers revenue faster than a subscription business would, and the issuer itself says usage-based revenue is more immediately affected. Contracted visibility is thin, with remaining performance obligations equal to 2.07% of annual revenue. Pricing power is mixed: gross margin held at 49% in FY2025 against 51% in FY2024 while growth was 14%, but some competitors have lower list prices and carrier fee increases were passed through at cost, so revenue growth excluding those fees was 12.55% in FY2025 and 15.84% in the latest quarter. Revenue is therefore cyclical and discretionary at the margin, concentrated in Messaging at 56.80%, and not structurally declining.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 19, 26, 30, 84, 87, 90, 92, 110, 136; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 29, 32; calculation C08; calculation C03; calculation C04; calculation C05
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Cost of revenue is mostly fees paid to network service providers, so gross margin follows carrier and cloud pricing, and pass-through of higher carrier fees raises revenue and cost equally, which dilutes margin without changing gross profit. Operating expenses consist primarily of personnel costs: they were 45.80% of revenue in FY2025 against 52.31% in FY2024, so derived EBITDA rose with gross profit and the incremental operating margin in nine months 2026 was 31.38%. Margins can be defended against volume pressure only partly: a fall of 18.94% in gross profit would remove all derived EBITDA with costs unchanged, but management has cut costs before, reducing sales and marketing expense by 15.85% from FY2023 to FY2024, which is the lever that would be used first.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 83, 87–89; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3; calculation C14; calculation C16; calculation C18; calculation C17
### Capital intensity and FCF conversion

Capital intensity is low: capitalized software and long-lived asset purchases were 1.14% of FY2025 revenue, and cash taxes were only USD 25.74 million in nine months 2026, so almost all operating cash flow is free cash flow, USD 945 million in FY2025 and USD 1.11 billion for the last twelve months. The conversion is flattered by stock-based compensation, which is 11.85% of revenue; after it free cash flow was USD 345 million in FY2025 and USD 525 million for the last twelve months. Cash interest of about USD 37.5 million a year is covered 14.30x by derived EBITDA, so debt service is not the constraint on free cash flow; share repurchases and the commitments are.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 93, 107; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 6; calculation C30; calculation C23; calculation C24; calculation C26; calculation C34; calculation C29
### Porter's Five Forces

Rivalry is real and rising: the issuer names CPaaS companies, regional carriers with developer tools, customer-experience and customer-data vendors as rivals, expects competition to intensify, and says some rivals have lower list prices, which if matched would lower gross profit against a fixed cost base. Entry pressure comes at the edges, since new market entrants and software vendors target parts of the product line, but breadth across messaging, voice, email and data is not matched by any one rival, which protects the core. Substitutes are the sharpest threat to authentication and messaging volumes, for example if one-time passwords are phased out or over-the-top channels such as WhatsApp and RCS shift traffic, although Twilio sells those channels itself. Buyer power is limited by diversification, with the ten largest accounts at 9% of revenue, but developers can switch and may reduce or delay spending. Supplier power is high: carriers and one cloud provider are hard to replace, many carriers have no long-term contracts, and fee rises are passed on only to the extent customers accept them.
### PEST analysis

Four factors alter credit capacity. Regulatory exposure is real but contained: Twilio ended service to Iran-linked entities in March 2025 without receiving revenue from them, and telecommunications, privacy and sanctions rules govern its channels. Economic exposure is the usage model, which the issuer says is more immediately hit by weak macro conditions, tariffs and inflation than subscription revenue. Technological change cuts both ways, since AI products and new channels such as RCS add volume while changes to authentication practice could reduce it. Political factors act through trade policy and sanctions risk, with no figure that moves the credit view.
### SWOT analysis

- **Strengths:** net cash with cash and securities of USD 2.89 billion against USD 1.0 billion of notes; free cash flow of USD 945 million in FY2025; a broad customer base with expansion of 108%; and low capital intensity of 1.14% of revenue.

- **Weaknesses:** derived EBITDA margin of 9.20% on the last twelve months; usage-based revenue with contracted visibility of 2.07%; supplier dependence on carriers and one cloud provider; and repurchases not limited by the notes' summarised terms.

- **Opportunities that could improve credit quality:** further operating leverage, as shown by the incremental operating margin of 31.38%; and new channels and AI-related products that lift usage at similar margins.

- **Threats that could weaken credit quality:** further carrier fee increases that customers do not absorb; price competition from rivals with lower list prices; and a debt-funded buyback or acquisition.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12, 30, 34, 84, 87, 107, 135–136; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 8; calculation C35; calculation C30; calculation C13; calculation C08; calculation C16
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are strong in the sense that matters to creditors: USD 5.07 billion of revenue, many customers and a platform the issuer says no single rival matches in breadth. Competitive advantage is average, because it rests on breadth, deliverability and integration rather than contracts, and the filings supply no market share or switching evidence beyond expansion of 108%. Diversification is average: customers and geography are spread, with the ten largest at 9% and International at 36%, but Messaging is 56.80% of revenue. Cost and capex flexibility is strong, with 1.14% capital intensity and a record of cost cuts. Margin stability is weak: gross margin moved from 49% to 51% and back to 49%, and derived EBITDA margin is 9.20%. Free cash flow stability is average, because the cash is reliable but USD 41 million of it remained after stock-based compensation in FY2024. Refinancing and market access is strong given the 2.89x cash cover and the 2029 maturity. Liquidity is strong, with USD 2.89 billion of cash and securities and no facility to refinance or draw. Financial policy and governance is average: no debt-funded distribution and a clean audit, but large repurchases and unknown indenture limits and board detail. The trend is improving on leverage and margin, with the main missing items being the indenture, the commitment schedule and competitor data.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12, 84, 87, 90, 92, 101, 107, 135–136; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 13; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C05; calculation C30; calculation C13; calculation C25; calculation C35; calculation C36
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the evidence favours continued cash generation: revenue grew 20% in the latest quarter, or 15.84% excluding carrier fees, expansion was 114%, and operating expenses rose only 3.51% in the quarter against revenue growth of 20%. Headwinds are that pass-through revenue dilutes margin, purchase commitments of USD 1.3 billion call on cash, repurchases continue, and the Syniverse stake still produces losses. Over three to five years the 2029 and 2031 notes fall due, and the cash cushion means they can be repaid or refinanced on the issuer's terms; the tailwind is rising usage by existing customers, as the expansion rate shows, and new channels such as RCS, and the headwind is price competition and possible substitution of one-time passwords. No forecast or guidance was supplied, so this outlook extrapolates reported trends.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 19, 26, 30; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 15, 32–33; calculation C04; calculation C15
### Downside scenario

The initiating condition is a further round of carrier fee increases that customers resist, combined with price competition in messaging. The first operational break is gross margin: cost of revenue, mostly network fees, rises faster than revenue, so gross profit falls. The financial transmission is fast because operating expenses are largely fixed; with operating costs unchanged, a 10% fall in last-twelve-month gross profit takes derived EBITDA from USD 537 million to USD 253 million, lifts total debt to derived EBITDA to 3.92x and cuts cover to 6.75x, and a fall of 18.94% would remove all derived EBITDA. Free cash flow would fall by the same amount before tax effects, to about USD 827 million, which still covers cash interest many times over. The liquidity and refinancing consequence is limited: cash and securities of USD 2.89 billion cover the notes 2.89x before any free cash flow, nothing falls due until 2029, and management could stop repurchases, which have USD 698.7 million of authorisation left, or cut sales and marketing cost as in 2024. Resilience therefore appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress; the observable triggers are gross profit falling while revenue grows, cash and securities falling towards USD 2.0 billion, and repurchases above free cash flow. This is an illustration labelled as analyst judgement, not a forecast.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34, 83, 87, 89; 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 13, 39; calculation C18; calculation C19; calculation C20; calculation C21; calculation C22; calculation C36
### Strengths and weaknesses

The main strengths are balance-sheet and cash strength: net cash on cash and equivalents alone, USD 2.89 billion of cash and securities against notes of USD 1.0 billion, free cash flow of USD 945 million in FY2025, a customer base with no concentration and expansion of 108%, and recovered margins with an incremental operating margin of 31.38%.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_twlo-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2, 3, 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_twlo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 84, 87, 93; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C35; calculation C16; calculation C24

The main weaknesses are thin derived margins and low contract visibility, dependence on carriers and one cloud provider with fee increases passed on at cost, Messaging at 56.80% of revenue, a shareholder-return policy that the notes' summarised terms do not limit, and purchase commitments of USD 1.3 billion that are reported without a schedule.
